title: Inspection and scope
audience: Carpet and upholstery cleaners who inspect the item and agree the scope before work.
referencesAtStart: Official sources: Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC), False or misleading claims (no date in the body; page metadata shows 28 June 2026); Safe Work Australia, Model Code of Practice: Hazardous manual tasks (no date or edition shown).
learningOutcomes: Inspect the carpet or upholstery for soil, stains, wear, colour change and damage before work.
Agree the scope, the limits and the known risks with the customer in writing.
Record items that the cleaning cannot be expected to remove.

instruction.heading: Inspect in good light, from several angles
instruction.body: Inspect the item in good light, and walk it or move around it so that you see it from more than one angle. A raking light, a torch held low across the surface, shows the pile direction, flattened traffic lanes and marks that a flat light hides. Look at the traffic lanes, the high-use areas near doors and stairs, the edges and the areas under furniture where the customer allows furniture to be moved. An inspection done only from the doorway misses most of the soil that the customer cares about. Note the soil, the stains, the wear, any colour change, fading, seam damage, loose edges and any pre-existing marks, and check for odour. Photograph the condition with the customer's permission, and include a reference object so that the size of a mark can be judged later.

instruction.heading: Separate soil, stains, wear and damage
instruction.body: Soil is the loose or embedded dirt that cleaning is expected to remove. Stains are marks that have a source, such as food, drink, oil, ink or dye, and each responds differently to the same method. Wear is the loss of pile height or colour where the item is walked on, sat on or rubbed, and cleaning cannot restore lost pile. Colour change includes fading and dye movement, and it can be permanent. Damage includes burns, tears, cuts, shrinkage, delamination of the backing and failed seams. Record each one separately. Any sign of wetness that has not dried, a musty smell or visible growth is not routine soil; it is a moisture or biological concern, and it is handled as set out below.

instruction.heading: Agree the scope and the limits in writing
instruction.body: Agree the scope in writing before work starts. The scope covers the areas to be cleaned, the method, the result the customer can reasonably expect and the limits. State plainly that some stains and wear may not come out, that colour change or fibre damage may be permanent, and that the result is assessed after the clean. Do not promise a result that the inspection does not support, and do not let the customer's hope stand in for the evidence. Where the customer wants more than the inspection supports, say so, record the difference, and offer a specialist assessment or a separate job. The signed scope is the document that protects both parties when the result is discussed later.

instruction.heading: Claims about results need a basis
instruction.body: Any statement about what the cleaning will achieve is a claim, and it needs a basis. The ACCC guidance expects a business that speaks about a future matter to have its grounds in place when it speaks, and to be able to show them later (ACCC, False or misleading claims, fetched 2026-11-03). The same guidance cautions against forecasts that lack firm support. In practice, a phrase such as removes everything, or guaranteed, is not used unless there is evidence for it. The page does not name those particular words, so the test is the basis, not the word. Keep a note of the basis for the result you describe, such as the inspection, the test and the product information.

instruction.heading: Record what cleaning cannot be expected to remove
instruction.body: Record items that cleaning cannot be expected to remove, such as old dye stains that have set into the fibre, pet damage, scorch or burn marks, bleach marks, and permanent colour loss. Record items that need a specialist, such as repairs, re-stretching of loose carpet, and fabric replacement. Refer any mould, moisture or biological contamination to a qualified service, and do not treat it as routine cleaning. Stop and do not disturb any suspected contamination until the referral has been made and recorded.

instruction.heading: Moving furniture and manual handling
instruction.body: Inspection often means moving furniture, rolling up rugs or lifting an upholstered item. Safe Work Australia's model Code of Practice on hazardous manual tasks says that manual tasks must be identified, that their risks must be assessed, and that the risks must be managed. In practice, plan the lift, ask for help with heavy or awkward items, use the equipment you have, and do not move anything that you cannot control.

procedure: Inspect the item in good light from more than one angle, including the traffic lanes, the high-use areas and the edges.
Note soil, stains, wear, colour change, fading, seam damage, odour and pre-existing marks, and keep each one separate.
Photograph the condition with the customer's permission, with a reference object in frame.
Agree the scope, method, expected result and limits in writing, and state what may not come out.
Record the basis for any result you describe, and remove any claim that the evidence does not support.
Record items outside the cleaning, and refer any suspected mould, moisture or biological contamination before any further work.
Date and sign the inspection record, and give the customer a copy.

workedExamples.situation: A client expects an old red wine stain on a cream carpet to disappear completely before a family event.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you agree, and what do you record before any product is used?
workedExamples.reasoning: Inspect the stain in good light and record its size, its edge, its colour and its age as the client describes it. Photograph it with a reference object in the frame. Explain that some stains may not fully come out, that the fibre may show a change in colour, and that the result is assessed after the clean. Agree in writing that the result will be assessed after the clean and that full removal is not promised. Do not say that the stain will disappear, because the inspection does not support that claim.

workedExamples.situation: (Example job) During an inspection of a sofa cushion, a musty smell and a faint dark area are found along the seam at the back. The owner asks for the cushion to be cleaned as routine so it looks fresh for guests.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Do you clean it as routine, and what do you record?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not clean it as routine. A musty smell and a dark area at a seam can mean moisture or growth, which is not routine soil. Record the location, the photographs taken with permission, and the owner's statement. Refer the item to a qualified service for assessment, and tell the owner that the routine clean is on hold until the referral is answered. Do not disturb the area with heavy wetting while the referral is pending.

workedExamples.situation: (Example job) A customer asks for a written guarantee that a set-in dye stain on a fabric armchair will never return after cleaning.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you write in the scope?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not write the guarantee. Record the stain and the inspection, and write what the cleaning is expected to achieve in terms the inspection supports. State that the dye may not lift, that it may move during cleaning, and that a further assessment can be offered separately. Keep the basis for the description in the job file, as the ACCC guidance expects a business to be able to show the grounds for a claim.

equipmentAndPpe: Inspection torch, used low across the surface, and a magnifier
Camera or phone for photographs, used only with the customer's permission, with a reference object
Gloves for handling furniture, rugs and any item that may be wet or soiled
Moisture check method approved by the business, where a reading is needed
No handling of a suspected mould or biological area without the referral set out in the lesson

commonErrors.prevention: Walk the item, check the traffic lanes and edges, and look under furniture where the customer allows it to be moved.

commonErrors.error: Promising full removal of an old stain.
commonErrors.prevention: Describe the likely outcome in terms the inspection supports, and agree the limits in writing.

commonErrors.error: Treating suspected mould, a musty smell or a damp seam as routine cleaning.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop, record the location, and refer the item to a qualified service before any further work.

commonErrors.error: Making a claim about the result with no basis on file.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep the inspection, the test and the product information that support each result you describe.

commonErrors.error: Agreeing the scope verbally and recording it after the work.
commonErrors.prevention: Sign the scope and limits before the first treatment.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Suspected mould, moisture or biological contamination is outside routine cleaning and may need specialist assessment.

A business that predicts a result is expected to have its grounds in place when it makes the statement, and to be able to show them (ACCC, False or misleading claims). Forecasts that lack firm support are also cautioned against.
Furniture moving and lifting are manual tasks. Safe Work Australia's model Code of Practice on hazardous manual tasks says that the risks must be identified, assessed and managed.
The content is general cleaning practice and needs subject-matter and regulator review before use.

qualityStandard: Inspection completed from several angles, including the traffic lanes and the edges, in the practical.
Soil, stains, wear, colour change and damage recorded as separate items, with photographs taken with permission.
Scope, limits and exclusions agreed and signed before work in the simulated job.
Suspected mould or moisture referred and recorded, not cleaned as routine, in the simulated job.
documentationEvidence: Pre-work inspection record, with dated photographs where permitted
Signed scope, limits and exclusions form
Referral record for any suspected mould, moisture or biological contamination
Note of the basis for each result described to the customer
summary: Inspect from several angles, including the traffic lanes, the edges and, with permission, under furniture.
Agree the scope and its limits in writing before the first treatment.
Support every claim about a result with a basis you can show.
Record what cleaning cannot remove, and refer any suspected mould or moisture.

knowledgeChecks.question: Where must the inspection be done?
options: From the doorway only, since that gives the best overall view of the whole room and every stain
Across the traffic lanes and the edges, from several angles, with permission for areas under furniture
Only on the stain itself, since that is the one area the client is concerned about and wants checked

knowledgeChecks.question: A client expects a stain to disappear completely. What is correct?
options: Promise that it will disappear, since the cleaner has the right method
Explain the likely limit and agree it in writing after the inspection
Say nothing about the limit, so the client stays happy with the job

knowledgeChecks.question: Suspected mould is found in the carpet. What is correct?
options: Clean it as routine, since it is only a small patch of soil
Hide it with a rug, so the client does not see it
Stop, record it, and refer it to a qualified service

knowledgeChecks.question: What must a business have when it makes a claim about a future result?
options: Only the customer's hope that the result will happen, since the customer is paying for it
A reasonable basis at the time the claim is made, which it must be able to show
Nothing, if the customer signs a form that takes all the risk for the result
